evaluation.positioning_hook: A sorority freshman and her grocery-store best friend go undercover as frat boys to expose a campus predator, turning rush week into a savage gender-swap takedown.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and built for broad conversation: college party culture, sexual misconduct, and undercover gender play all have clear audience entry points. The opening assault, the rush-week infiltration, and the final campus-wide fallout give it a strong commercial engine.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening pages and never stops being easy to explain: two women infiltrate a frat as men to trap the guy who assaulted one of them. The story engine is clean, specific, and escalates through a series of clear set pieces.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Daisy and Maddy are sharply contrasted and playable: one is wounded and determined, the other is combative, funny, and socially fluent in a different way. Brad, Tanner, Jake, Stephanie, and Courtney all have distinct comic functions, and the Daisy/Maddy bond carries the movie.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script commits hard to a risky comic premise and keeps finding new angles on it, especially once the undercover scheme becomes a full social experiment in masculinity. The tonal confidence in mixing assault accountability, frat absurdism, and gender performance gives it a real point of view.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The movie keeps generating forward motion through reversals, disguises, and escalating infiltration beats, with the rush process functioning as a built-in ladder. The Jungle-party climax and the final confession sequence pay off the setup with real propulsion.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels fresh because it fuses a campus assault story with a gender-disguise comedy and a frat-house takedown. The undercover mechanics are specific enough to feel inevitable once you see them, which is exactly why they play.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Greek life is rendered as a complete ecosystem with its own rituals, language, status games, and institutional cover-ups. The sorority, the frat, Title 9, campus police, Nationals, and the grocery-store job all create a lived-in social map.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very identifiable voice: filthy, fast, self-aware, and willing to swing from crude jokes to genuine anger without losing its comic identity. The dialogue rhythms, running bits, and repeated frat/sorority inversions make the tone easy to recognize.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the comedy, the script is tracking belief, complicity, and the social cost of being heard, especially in the Daisy/Courtney and Daisy/Maddy dynamics. The ending’s campus-wide ripple effects suggest a larger thematic world beyond the central takedown.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Daisy-Maddy-Tanner triangle, the Daisy-Brad-Courtney knot, and the Daisy-Jake-Stephanie crosscurrents all generate independent scenes and comic pressure. The ensemble is active enough that multiple pairings can drive set pieces without the movie collapsing onto one lead.

casting_characteristics: Several roles require strong comedic timing and physical comedy

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond simple title cards and possible cleanup for party crowd continuity.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical vomit gag, fire gag for the wig, pepper spray beat, beer pong and party chaos, cattle-brand prosthetic makeup/effects.

rights_flags.detail: Mo Bamba, John Mayer, Troye Sivan, Chappell Roan, Waka Flocka, and other named/clear-reference music cues are referenced in dialogue and scene direction.
Jose Cuervo, Market Basket, Zara, McKinsey, and other branded references appear on the page.
Gloria Steinem is referenced in dialogue.
Ryan Reynolds is referenced in dialogue.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: streaming theatrical-comedy lane / premium streamer feature
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong festival-to-platform or streamer-first potential; the engine is the undercover rush-week takedown and campus fallout.

cost.note: Contemporary college settings, a contained cast, and mostly practical party/interior scenes keep the budget in a modest feature range.

cast.note: The movie depends on four strong young leads plus a sizable college ensemble, and the gender-disguise material asks for performers with sharp comic control.

location.note: The story moves through frat, sorority, campus, grocery store, house, and van spaces, but all are contemporary and producible.

content.note: Sexual assault, drugging, explicit language, and hazing imagery narrow the lane and require careful platform and marketing alignment.

rights.note: The script uses several named songs, brands, and public figures, which creates a meaningful clearance pass but not an IP-dependent premise.

strengths.what_it_means: This is the kind of feature a buyer can understand in one breath, which helps it travel from a manager’s inbox to a greenlight meeting without translation. It will attract producers looking for a clean high-concept comedy with a topical engine and a clear audience hook.
strengths.evidence: Daisy and Maddy literally go undercover as frat guys to get close to Brad and force a confession.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Daisy and Maddy are a real comic engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The movie has a built-in two-hander dynamic: Daisy brings wounded urgency, Maddy brings swagger and bite, and their friendship gives the comedy emotional ballast. That kind of lead pairing is catnip for actresses who want a showcase and for buyers who want a movie that can live on chemistry.
strengths.evidence: Their ping-pong banter, secret handshake, and constant bickering while executing the plan keep the movie alive.

strengths.what_it_means: The script doesn’t just do one disguise gag and move on; it turns the premise into a full social experiment about how men move through the world. That gives the film repeatable set pieces and a trailer-friendly escalation path.
strengths.evidence: The wigs, sock-dicks, man-walk training, confidence drills, and rush rituals all build the same joke into a bigger machine.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Greek life is treated like a closed ecosystem.
strengths.what_it_means: The frat and sorority worlds have enough rules, rituals, and status games to feel like a mini-society, which makes the setting more than a backdrop. That density gives producers a world that can support repeat viewing and strong word-of-mouth because the details feel lived-in.
strengths.evidence: Rush, pledging, Nationals, the Tiki Bar, Jungle, Honor Council, and Title 9 all operate as part of the same social machine.

strengths.dimension_or_area: It has a sharp, saleable tonal identity.
strengths.what_it_means: The script lives in a lane that blends raunchy comedy, campus satire, and real anger without losing momentum, which is a useful brand position in the current feature market. Buyers who want edgy but accessible comedy will see a clear lane for it.
strengths.evidence: The script swings from vomit jokes and sock-dicks to Title 9 hearings, drink spiking, and a final confession scene.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The supporting cast keeps generating story.
strengths.what_it_means: Brad, Courtney, Tanner, Jake, Stephanie, Olivia, Kendall, and the frat brothers all have enough personality to create multiple pairings and reversals, which makes the movie feel bigger than a single revenge plot. That ensemble energy is attractive to directors and buyers who want a comedy with rewatchable side characters.
strengths.evidence: Courtney’s shift from rival to ally, Jake’s romantic confusion, Tanner’s coaching role, and the frat brothers’ evolving reactions all create independent scenes.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending broadens the movie’s payoff.
strengths.what_it_means: The final stretch doesn’t just resolve the central conflict; it shows the social fallout across campus, which makes the movie feel like it matters beyond the last scene. That kind of ending helps a producer sell the film as both a crowd-pleaser and a conversation starter.
strengths.evidence: The campus-wide complaints, DIK getting kicked off campus, and the girls organizing against the house all extend the impact.

whats_special.headline: RUSH is a filthy, fast, and highly marketable college comedy with a real engine: two women weaponize frat-boy behavior to expose the predator at the center of campus life. It has the kind of clean premise, strong lead chemistry, and built-in escalation that can sell on concept while still landing as a crowd-pleasing ensemble movie.

lead_characters.name: DAISY
lead_characters.hook: Daisy is the movie’s emotional center: a golden-girl freshman who starts out trying to outrun what happened to her and ends up turning rage into strategy. She’s funny, image-conscious, and deeply wounded, with a voice that can snap from flirty to feral in a beat; the role lives in the contradiction between her polished sorority exterior and the private panic underneath it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Carey Mulligan in Promising Young Woman — a woman whose charm and precision are the weapon, and whose pain keeps changing the temperature of every scene. An actress gets comedy, vulnerability, and righteous propulsion in one part, which is exactly the kind of role that can redefine how the industry sees her.

lead_characters.name: MADDY
lead_characters.hook: Maddy is Daisy’s best friend and the movie’s chaos engine: tomboyish, sharp-tongued, socially fearless, and secretly more emotionally invested than she lets on. She can read a room, read a person, and read a sorority girl’s entire life in one line, which makes her both a comic assassin and the perfect undercover partner.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase space of Kristen Wiig in Bridesmaids — a fast-talking comic lead who can make selfishness, loyalty, and panic all feel alive in the same scene. It’s a part for an actress who can do big laughs while still landing the ache of being the friend who always shows up first.

lead_characters.name: TANNER
lead_characters.hook: Tanner is the older-brother wildcard: a reformed frat guy, local-business adult, and accidental masculinity coach who is still emotionally stuck in the college ecosystem. He’s funny because he takes the boys’ code seriously enough to teach it, and useful because he knows exactly how the machine works from the inside.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Paul Rudd in a broad ensemble comedy — the charming adult who can play clueless, supportive, and unexpectedly useful without ever losing likability. It gives a comic actor a chance to be the bridge between the women’s plan and the frat world, which is a very playable lane.

lead_characters.name: BRAD
lead_characters.hook: Brad is the movie’s charismatic predator: handsome, socially fluent, and always performing the version of himself that gets him what he wants. He’s funniest when he’s most dangerous, because he can pivot from golden-boy charm to manipulative gaslighting to full collapse without ever leaving the same smiley surface.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Penn Badgley in You or Billy Crudup in The Morning Show — a polished, self-justifying man whose charm is inseparable from menace. It’s the kind of role that lets an actor play seduction, entitlement, and cowardice in one package, which is catnip for prestige-leaning genre casting.

lead_characters.name: JAKE
lead_characters.hook: Jake is the sweet, awkward freshman who keeps stumbling into the movie’s emotional crossfire. He’s earnest enough to be funny and confused enough to be dangerous, which makes him a useful romantic foil and a believable product of the frat ecosystem without being fully corrupted by it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Lucas Hedges in a coming-of-age ensemble — the sensitive guy whose sincerity creates both comedy and pathos. A young actor gets to play romantic longing, social awkwardness, and the slow realization that he’s been standing in the wrong room.

lead_characters.name: STEPHANIE
lead_characters.hook: Stephanie is the ethereal sorority girl who starts as a romantic object and ends up becoming one of the movie’s clearest moral voices. She’s smart, funny, and more self-possessed than the men around her realize, which lets the script flip her from fantasy to ally without losing her appeal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Zoey Deutch in a sharp campus comedy — the girl who can be glamorous, funny, and emotionally legible in the same scene. It gives an actress the chance to play the moment a character stops being decorative and starts steering the room.

lead_characters.name: COURTNEY
lead_characters.hook: Courtney begins as the polished rival and evolves into a complicated ally whose anger has been sitting under the surface the whole time. She’s socially sharp, image-aware, and capable of both cruelty and solidarity, which makes her one of the movie’s best late-game pivots.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Alison Brie in a sharp ensemble comedy — a character who can weaponize status, then reveal hurt, then swing back into action. It’s a juicy part for an actress who likes playing intelligence with a little venom.

lead_characters.name: OLIVIA
lead_characters.hook: Olivia is the grounded friend who sees more than she says and gives the sorority side of the story a practical spine. She’s less performative than Daisy or Maddy, which makes her useful as a reality-check character and a quiet source of solidarity.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded supporting role that works in the Allison Janney / Auli’i Cravalho lane of ensemble specificity — not the loudest voice, but the one that makes the group feel real. It gives an actor clean, scene-stealing reactions and a credible emotional anchor.

lead_characters.name: KENDALL
lead_characters.hook: Kendall is the other half of the sorority trio: skeptical, observant, and funny in a dry, slightly wounded way. She helps the movie widen beyond Daisy and Maddy by showing how the women around them are also negotiating loyalty, fear, and social pressure.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp supporting role that gives an actor the dry-comic lane of a Jenny Slate ensemble part — quick, specific, and memorable without needing to carry the whole plot. It’s a great fit for someone who can make a single look land like a punchline.

lead_characters.name: HARRISON
lead_characters.hook: Harrison is the frat president who takes the whole absurd system with deadly seriousness. He’s a comic bureaucrat of masculinity, which makes him useful as both a gatekeeper and a punchline whenever the movie wants to show how institutional the frat culture really is.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a deadpan ensemble player like Zach Woods — the guy who can make institutional stupidity feel almost noble. It gives an actor a chance to play authority as a joke that the movie keeps exposing.

lead_characters.name: ANGELO
lead_characters.hook: Angelo is the frat brother with the most open heart and the least self-awareness, which makes him both funny and strangely sympathetic. He’s the kind of guy who can be swept up by the group’s logic while still feeling like a real person rather than a pure caricature.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a comic supporting player like Tony Revolori in a campus ensemble — eager, impressionable, and always one beat away from embarrassment. It gives an actor a chance to play loyalty and cluelessness at the same time.

lead_characters.name: THEO
lead_characters.hook: Theo is the film-bro frat guy who thinks he’s the smartest person in the room and is usually wrong in a very specific way. He’s a great pressure-release valve because his self-mythology is so transparent, yet the script keeps him useful inside the group dynamic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a scene-stealing indie comic like Ben Schwartz — fast, self-regarding, and always one smug line away from humiliation. It gives an actor a chance to play performative intelligence as a running joke.

lead_characters.name: PRESTON
lead_characters.hook: Preston is the moneyed frat archetype: polished, entitled, and always talking like the world was built to accommodate him. He helps define the class texture of the house and gives the movie another flavor of male privilege to puncture.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a wealthy-prep comic type like Will Poulter in a satire — the guy whose entitlement is funny because it’s so specific. It’s a clean supporting slot for an actor who can make privilege feel embodied rather than generic.

lead_characters.name: TOMMY
lead_characters.hook: Tommy is one of the frat’s functional background brothers, useful as part of the house’s social machinery and the casual normalization of the culture. He helps the movie feel populated by a real ecosystem rather than a handful of named villains.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of small but vivid ensemble slot that working comedy actors use to make a world feel lived-in, similar to the utility roles in a Judd Apatow ensemble. It’s a good fit for a performer who can land a line and disappear back into the crowd.

lead_characters.name: MANAGER
lead_characters.hook: The Market Basket manager is the everyday authority figure who keeps Maddy’s world grounded outside the frat plot. He’s part of the movie’s class texture, showing that the women’s lives are not just campus-bound performance spaces.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded supporting role that gives a character actor a few sharp beats in a broader comedy, like the store managers and bosses in a Nicole Holofcener ensemble. It’s a clean fit for someone who can make ordinary authority feel specific.

lead_characters.name: BUREAUCRAT
lead_characters.hook: The Title 9 bureaucrat is the face of institutional delay and procedural absurdity. He’s not a villain in a big theatrical sense; he’s worse in a more realistic way, because he turns Daisy’s trauma into paperwork and timing.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of a dry institutional comic role like the administrators in The Office or the hearing-room officials in a prestige satire. It gives an actor a chance to play passive obstruction as comedy.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a filthy campus comedy with real social teeth.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Second- or third-feature directors with festival-comedy or sharp ensemble experience, especially those who like performance-forward material and can balance raunch with point of view. This is for a filmmaker who understands how to stage social humiliation, undercover reversals, and crowd scenes without flattening the emotional stakes.
director_appeal.detail: The material rewards directors who can keep the comedy moving while letting the assault accountability story stay legible and emotionally grounded. It also gives a director a chance to build a very marketable ensemble movie with repeatable set pieces, strong party visuals, and a clear tonal signature.

buyer_appeal.lane: premium streamer comedy / edgy campus satire
buyer_appeal.detail: It can be cast off four strong young leads and a supporting ensemble, so it does not require star-level attachments to function. The contemporary college setting, contained locations, and topical premise make it exportable and easy to position as a conversation-starting comedy with trailer-friendly set pieces.

considerations.area: The opening assault is the movie’s hardest turn.
considerations.detail: The script is clear about what happened, but the first pages ask the audience to move from party comedy into assault immediately. One lever would be to let Daisy’s social world breathe a little longer before the inciting event, so the emotional whiplash lands with even more force and the audience knows exactly what she loses.

considerations.area: The confession engine repeats in several forms.
considerations.detail: The movie keeps returning to the same objective — get Brad to admit it — through Title 9, the frat infiltration, and the final bedroom scene. A next pass could sharpen the distinction between those attempts so each one reveals a new layer of the world rather than re-running the same pressure in a different outfit.

considerations.area: The undercover mechanics are the movie’s biggest asset.
considerations.detail: The disguise material is the engine, so the version of the script where each phase of the plan has a slightly different social rule would make the escalation even cleaner. That would protect the comedy and make the final Jungle sequence feel like the inevitable summit of everything the movie has been teaching us.

considerations.area: The named-music and brand references are plentiful.
considerations.detail: The script leans on a lot of specific songs, brands, and pop-culture references, which gives it texture but also means the clearance pass will matter. A producer could preserve the energy by keeping the cultural specificity while being open to swaps where needed.

considerations.area: The party footprint is manageable but active.
considerations.detail: Most of the movie lives in contemporary interiors and night exteriors around campus, frat, sorority, and house spaces, so the production is contained even with a lively crowd feel. The version that consolidates a few of the campus beats into fewer repeatable locations would protect the pace while keeping the budget in the sweet spot.
